items.title: SSMs had the nice asymptotics but kept missing out on the inference goodies Transformers get for fre...
items.content: SSMs had the nice asymptotics but kept missing out on the inference goodies Transformers get for free like spec decode and quantization. Turns out we were just not caching the right thing. Same IO-aware trick behind FlashAttention, Mamba scan, paged KV. A lot of the big wins weren’t new architectures, just people taking memory IO seriously.
items.author: @tri_dao
items.summary: Following yesterday's [Research](/?date=2026-10-12&category=research#item-d7b864918789) on ReplaySSM, Tri Dao shares the broader lesson, Tri Dao reflects that SSMs' failure to benefit from inference optimizations like speculative decoding and quantization was due to caching the wrong things, arguing that the same IO-aware memory principle behind FlashAttention, Mamba scan, and paged KV caching explains the biggest wins, which came from taking memory IO seriously rather than new architectures.

items.title: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, achieving Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index...
items.content:
Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, achieving Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 scores of 52 and 56 at max reasoning effort - each a material gain over Muse Spark 1.3 (max) at 48, with a release gap of only 6 weeks

Muse Wonder is available for users on Meta’s first-party API, while Muse Wonder Full is currently only available for Muse Code users. Meta notes that each model is designed for personal and professional agent use

Congratulations to @AIatMeta, @finkd, and @alexandr_wang on the release!

Key Takeaways:

➤ Both models exhibit a material jump in overall Intelligence Index score. Muse Wonder Full (max) improves on Muse Spark 1.3 (max) across all ten Intelligence Index evaluations, gaining 8 points to 56. The largest gains were seen in agentic evaluations: Terminal-Bench 4.0 (+24 points, 33% to 57%), GDPval-AA v2.1 (+176 Elo, 1681 to 1857), and AA-Briefcase (+148 Elo, 1581 to 1729). Muse Wonder (max) gains 4 Intelligence Index points and lands at 52, with notable improvements vs. Muse Spark 1.3 (max) in Terminal-Bench 4.0 (33% to 52%) and AutomationBench-AA (58% to 68%)

➤ Muse Wonder Full (max) places in the top three on six of the ten Intelligence Index evaluations, and is particularly strong in agentic knowledge work and scientific reasoning. In agentic knowledge work, it narrowly leads on GDP.pdf (33%), ranks #2 on GDPval-AA v2.1 (1857 Elo), and #3 on both AA-Briefcase (1729 Elo) and AutomationBench-AA (71%). In scientific reasoning, it tops the CritPt leaderboard at 33% and ranks #3 on SciCode with 63%. This builds on the relative strengths of Muse Spark 1.3 (max), which also showed particular ability in these two domains

➤ Both models use fewer output tokens than Muse Spark 1.3 (max). Muse Wonder (max) and Muse Wonder Full (max) each use around 54k output tokens per Intelligence Index task, down ~10% from Muse Spark 1.3 (max, 60k). This usage is lower than similarly intelligent models Gemini 4 Argon (high, 62k) and Claude Fable 5.1 (max w/ fallback, 78k), but higher than GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 38k) and GPT-6 Astra (max, 27k). Muse Wonder Full (max) uses 16% fewer input tokens per Intelligence Index task than Muse Wonder (max) (6.44M vs 7.69M), meaning it is both more intelligent and more token-efficient

➤ Cost per Task for Muse Wonder (max) lands higher than most similarly intelligent models. Despite efficient output token use, premium API pricing ($4 per million input tokens, $20 per million output tokens) and high input token use (7.69M per task) push Muse Wonder (max)’s cost to $4.52 per Intelligence Index task. This is lower than Claude Fable 5.1 (max w/ fallback, $7.63), Claude Opus 5.5 (max w/ fallback, $5.98), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max w/ fallback, $5.46), but higher than GPT-6 Astra (max, $3.26), Gemini 4 Argon (high, $1.99), GPT-6.1 Sol (max, $0.72), and its predecessor Muse Spark 1.3 (max, $1.60). Per-token pricing is not currently available for Muse Wonder Full, so no Cost per Task figure can be estimated at this stage

➤ Both models gain significantly in Coding Agent performance. Muse Wonder Full achieves 68 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agents Index at max effort in Muse Code, alongside Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 (max, 68) and Opus 5.5 (max, 66). Muse Wonder (max) scores 63. These represent material gains over Muse Code with Muse Spark 1.3 (max), which scores 54

Other details for the two new models:

➤ Context windows: 1M tokens each, unchanged from Muse Spark 1.3
➤ Pricing: for Muse Wonder, $4 input / $0.20 cached input / $20 output per 1M tokens. Pricing per token is not yet announced for Muse Wonder Full
➤ Input modalities: text, image, video, and audio
➤ Output modalities: text
➤ Availability: Muse Wonder is available on Meta's first-party API and Muse Code at launch, while Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code users

items.title:
We have measured intelligence. Now it's time to see it.

We are launching AA-3D, our new benchmark f...
items.content:
We have measured intelligence. Now it's time to see it.

We are launching AA-3D, our new benchmark for how well AI models build interactive 3D scenes. Each model works as an agent in an offline sandbox and turns a written brief into a three.js web page. A human panel of judges compares pairs of scenes built from the same brief without knowing which model made which.

AA-3D details:

➤ 55 written briefs across seven domains, including landmarks, machines, living bodies, games, and space. Each brief says what the scene must show and how people should interact with it, and leaves the rest to the model

➤ Each model gets up to three hours and 250 turns. Its sandbox has Blender, Rapier physics, Python, a headless browser to test its own work, and a CC0 library of materials, 3D models, and characters

➤ Panelists spend at least 30 seconds with each scene before they vote. One comparison in every four is a validation check

➤ Over 10,000 counted votes from over 1,000 panelists rank 21 models by Elo, with 95% confidence intervals

Key findings:

➤ Four models are statistically tied at the top: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1194), Claude Opus 5.5 (1190), GPT-6 Astra (1165), and Claude Fable 5.1 (1131). The 95% confidence intervals of the other three overlap Claude Sonnet 5.5's

➤ AA-3D Elo rises with intelligence: each point on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is worth about 18 Elo (Pearson 0.92)

➤ The best-placed open weights models, Kimi K3 (982) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (977), rank 11th and 12th, more than 200 points behind first place

➤ A scene costs $0.20 to $32.08, depending on the model. The cheapest, GPT-6 Luna, ranks eighth

More results, more scenes, and how AA-3D works follow in the thread below.

items.title: We're launching our leaderboard for FrontierCode 1.1, a private evaluation from Cognition that tests...
items.content:
We're launching our leaderboard for FrontierCode 1.1, a private evaluation from Cognition that tests models on completing coding tasks in a way that would actually get merged by maintainers of real-world repositories

@cognition announced FrontierCode in June 2026 and updated it to version 1.1 in July. Cognition built the dataset with open source maintainers who spent more than 40 hours per task. Each task requires the agent to make a change to a real open source repository, then checks both unit tests and qualitative tests for what maintainers would require to merge the change.

We run FrontierCode 1.1 Main, the primary 100-task set of the benchmark's 150 tasks, using our Stirrup open source reference harness for apples-to-apples comparisons across models. All tasks are private to avoid contamination. Each attempt is graded with both blocking and non-blocking criteria. An attempt that fails any blocking check scores zero, and one that passes them all scores between 70% and 100%.

Unlike other coding evaluations, FrontierCode has a more holistic view of success based on real usage. Models need to pass unit tests, but are also assessed on behaviors like making excessive changes and large diffs, modifying files outside the relevant scope, or adding unhelpful tests. We think this approach is valuable in the current context: models are now very capable at coding tasks, but their changes can still require substantial cleanup before a maintainer would merge them.

Key takeaways:

➤ Leading models still fail more than 40% of the time: Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) leads at a score of 52% after passing blockers in 58% of its attempts. Nine of the 100 tasks were not passed in any attempt by any of the models we evaluated for launch

➤ The top of the leaderboard is tightly packed: nine models from six labs score between 43% and 52%. MiMo-V2.6-Pro is the leading open weights model at 45%, followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) and Kimi K3 (max) at 44%

➤ GPT-6.1 Sol (max) offers the strongest performance for its cost: At $0.81 per task it scores 49%, matching Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback). This means it achieves similar performance to leading Anthropic models, at less than a tenth of the cost per task

Thank you to @silasalberti, @ybenpan, @cl571128, and the rest of the team at Cognition for building FrontierCode and collaborating with us to bring it to Artificial Analysis - we’re working to add FrontierCode to our coding agent leaderboard very soon.

items.title: Every Perplexity Project is a Git repo. We built a Git forge for agents, without the GitHub bloat, s...
items.content:
Every Perplexity Project is a Git repo. We built a Git forge for agents, without the GitHub bloat, since no human has to approve anything.

Each agent gets its own short-lived sandbox and commits to a shared repo on S3. Fewer than 2% of submissions collide.

Agents search with plain `ls` and `grep`. That beats semantic search 63% vs 37% on answer accuracy for financial document analysis.

items.title: Cost per Task on FrontierCode spans two orders of magnitude, from $0.09 for GPT-6 Luna (max) to $12....
items.content:
Cost per Task on FrontierCode spans two orders of magnitude, from $0.09 for GPT-6 Luna (max) to $12.00 for Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback). Four models sit on the Pareto frontier for score vs. Cost per Task: GPT-6 Luna (max) at 42% and $0.09 per task, MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 45% and $0.18, GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 49% and $0.81, and Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) at 52% and $10.15.

GPT-6 models led on token efficiency in our testing. GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) averaged 27k and 33k output tokens per task respectively, compared with 157k for Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) and 236k for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback).

items.title: This is the best piece I’ve read to date on the Chinese data economy for LLMs, and how it compares t...
items.content:
This is the best piece I’ve read to date on the Chinese data economy for LLMs, and how it compares to the US counterparts (summarized by Mercor, Surge, and Handshake having the biggest network, SUPPLY, but also many companies with specialized services, in the form of RL-ready environments). China’s leading spenders, Tencent, Alibaba, and ByteDance, don’t mirror OpenAI and Anthropic leading the US market.

The Chinese market likely has a bias similar to their “ownership” mentality of more LLM builders in house, like Meituan, RedNote, and Xiaomi, whereas major US tech services build more on APIs and existing open-weight models.

Altogether, it seems like Chinese labs were 6–12 months behind on willingness to spend on data, relative to the US, but are rapidly catching up.

I've been hearing lots of murmurings on China's AI industry, but folks are secretive, so it's hard to put this all together.

items.title: We need a name for the kind of people that conflate 2022 pure LLMs that were in fact a tiny bit like...
items.content:
We need a name for the kind of people that conflate 2022 pure LLMs that were in fact a tiny bit like stochastic parrots (not my phrase, and not one I ever endorsed) with 2026 systems that couple those LLMs together with symbolic harnesses, code interpreters, and symbolic verification, typically to make a slippery rhetorical point.

Aside from being unfair to people who made a metaphor that applied (to some degree) to the technology of that time, it disrespects the innovations that were subsequently made and disrespects the critical contributions that neurosymbolic AI made to progress. 

What I hate most about this site is that so many people talk about AI yet few take any time to understand how the different underlying technologies work. Most prefer to make cheap rhetorical points instead.

Which is exactly why we are in the mess we are in.

items.title:
A very heated debate yesterday about this, which shows I hit a nerve

I asked @grok to summarize it ...
items.content:
A very heated debate yesterday about this, which shows I hit a nerve

I asked @grok to summarize it and it said people believe I am directionally correct but a bit early 

Which I agree with

It might take a few more years before everyone in the world uses AI chat apps and agents as @karpathy said

And also until most people understand what's actually possible with current and future AI models

But it's never bad to be early with these things and adapt before everyone else

One of the repeated misconceptions I see is that people think I mean people will ask AI agents to build software, but I don't, their AI agents will solve their problems by building software on the fly

With that a market springs up of software/data/etc for AI agents to pay for and connect to (like with MCP/APIs), but again the AI agents will try optimize to get the best service for the lowest price (free if possible) which makes it a cut-throat market, but possible to build a business in

Anyway, it's interesting times and I learnt a lot from the replies and quote tweets yesterday, thanks everyone!

items.title: I just met a quadriplegic who is working with a number of Austin companies doing BCI research. Brain...
items.content:
I just met a quadriplegic who is working with a number of Austin companies doing BCI research. Brain/Computer Interfaces. He lost control of his body in a surfing accident.

He just came out of a session with @phantom_neuro and said what they hooked up to his arm is the coolest thing he has ever used. Non invasive BCIs are quite amazing and Phantom is doing amazing work.

I wish I could say more (the company wants to keep its approach secret for now), but what he showed me shows that robotics and BCIs will change what it is like to be human very deeply. Eventually for all of us. 

I have a list of neuroscientists and BCI companies, so you can follow along. Will post that in replies.

Austin is a hotbed of this kind of research, with Neuralink being the one most people know about.

items.title: Muse Wonder Full (max) places in the top three on six of the ten Artificial Analysis Intelligence In...
items.content:
Muse Wonder Full (max) places in the top three on six of the ten Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3 evaluations:

➤ #1 on CritPt (33%) and GDP.pdf (33%)

➤ #2 on GDPval-AA v2.1 (1857 Elo)

➤ #3 on AA-Briefcase (1729 Elo), AutomationBench-AA (71%) and SciCode (63%)

The leads on CritPt and GDP.pdf are narrow, with the nearest competitors scoring 31-32%. On GDPval-AA v2.1, its result is within the confidence intervals of Claude Opus 5.5 (max w/ fallback, 1866) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max w/ fallback, 1838)

Its largest improvement over Muse Spark 1.3 is Terminal-Bench 4.0: 33% to 57%, bringing it level with Gemini 4 Argon (high)

items.title: Muse Wonder (max) costs $4.52 per Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index task, 2.8x Muse Spark 1.3 (...
items.content:
Muse Wonder (max) costs $4.52 per Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index task, 2.8x Muse Spark 1.3 (max, $1.60), driven by higher per-token prices and higher input token use

➤ Token pricing: $4 per 1M input tokens, $0.20 cached and $20 output, up from $1.25 / $0.15 / $4.25 for Muse Spark 1.3. This matches Claude Opus 5.5, is double each of Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-6.1 Sol ($2/$10), and is 60% below GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 ($10/$50)

➤ Input: 7.69M input tokens per task, 28% more than Muse Spark 1.3 (max, 6.03M) and 2-7x Gemini 4 Argon (high), GPT-6.1 Sol (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max). Input is $3.43 (76%) of its cost per task, composed of $1.92 cache writes, $1.44 cache hits and $0.07 uncached input

➤ Output: around 54k output tokens per task ($1.08), 10% fewer than Muse Spark 1.3 (max, 60k)

NEW: Meta released Muse Wonder (codenamed Watermelon), its new family of AI models, with scores that push the company to the frontier.

The top version, Wonder Full, scores 56 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, behind only Claude Opus 5.5 at 58.

It also leads rivals on:

- Legal work (Harvey LAB): 13.1 vs. 8.6 for GPT-6 Astra
- Long coding projects (SWE-Marathon): 57.5 vs. 46.3 for Opus 5.5
- Coding tasks (DeepSWE): 79.0 vs. 74.2 for Opus 5.5
- Remembering context (MemoryBench): 85.5 vs. 81.5 for Opus 5.5

Muse Wonder is live today in the Meta Model API and Muse Code, with Wonder Full open to paying Muse Code users.

items.title: I think one thing that's a bit dishonest that I saw a lot yesterday about the "software is dead" pos...
items.content:
I think one thing that's a bit dishonest that I saw a lot yesterday about the "software is dead" post and I don't blame them is people at all the AI companies kinda replying "omg yes it's the best time to build a startup ever" 

I mean yes, but you have to translate it to "omg best time to pay my company money for tokens to build your startup ever"

And you have a lot of people who are already rich (post-money) who say similar, because they don't need to pay their bills with their salary anymore

I'm also incentivized to say all this, half of my net worth is in AI stock (Google, SpaceX, Nvidia, and tech ETFs), I love to see their stock go up, but I care mostly about being real and no personally I don't think it's the best time to be in software ever, even if it's very unpopular to say this

I think it's definitely the best time ever for creativity, you can make things now you couldn't even imagine being possible to make just a few years ago, that doesn't necessarily translate to money though

There's ~40 million software developers in the world

There's 2 billion people regularly using AI tools now

So that's 50x, it'll grow to the same number as internet access, that's 6 billion people, so 200x more AI users than devs

Once AI agents can do the dev work (they already can), that means something for software, even if it's not right now, but it'll mean something in a few years

Many people predict this will cause the cost of everything to go down, and life will get cheaper, which is a good thing

It just doesn't mean as a software developer or entrepreneur you'll be paid for the same thing in the future you're paid for right now (maybe other moats, maybe UBI, etc)

items.content:
Knowledge remains a relative weakness for both models, but this is mitigated by very low hallucination rates. On AA-Omniscience, Muse Wonder Full (max) scores 30 and Muse Wonder (max) scores 25, level with Muse Spark 1.3 (max), below e.g. Claude Opus 5.5 (46), GPT-6 Astra (43), Gemini 4 Argon (42), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (32)

Muse Wonder Full (max)'s 5-point gain comes from lowering its hallucination rate (33% to 23%), which places it among the least-hallucinating models tested: it has the second-lowest hallucination rate of any model scoring 45 or more on the Intelligence Index, behind only Gemini 4 Argon (high, 15%). Muse Wonder (max) is third at 27%

items.title: Modern LLMs rely on the attention mechanism to process text, using Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE...
items.content:
Modern LLMs rely on the attention mechanism to process text, using Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) to track word order. However, these models suffer severe performance collapse when processing input sequences longer than their initial training context. While researchers previously attributed this failure to rotational values drifting out of distribution, the exact mechanical cause remained unexplained.

This article addresses this critical bottleneck by investigating why RoPE degrades over long inputs and establishing a unified geometric framework to resolve it.

• Agents can send feedback to your team

items.title: Modern AI applications increasingly demand processing long sequences of information, such as extensi...
items.content:
Modern AI applications increasingly demand processing long sequences of information, such as extensive documents or long-horizon tasks. However, training models directly on extreme sequence lengths requires prohibitive computing power and memory, and long-context training data remain scarce.

While recurrent architectures offer fixed-size memory that can theoretically run over arbitrarily long horizons at deployment, models trained on short sequences with standard backpropagation through time often fail to generalize to longer contexts. This breakdown limits our ability to adopt a cost-effective strategy of training on short sequences and deploying on long ones.

To overcome this limitation, this article from @Adobe  evaluates the mechanics of how learning signals propagate over time and introduces a training intervention called Credit Stabilization through Time. The main objective is to demonstrate that directly stabilizing "state credit"—the upstream supervisory signal through which future errors inform earlier internal memory states—enables recurrent sequence models trained on short contexts to extrapolate reliably to horizons up to 128 times longer.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/g8ILvwC7hG
items.author: @burkov
items.summary: Burkov summarizes an Adobe research article on long-context training for recurrent architectures, explaining how learning signals propagate over time and introducing a technique called Credit Stabilization through Time to stabilize state credit so models trained on short sequences generalize to longer contexts.
items.reasoning: Technically substantive summary of a research paper addressing a real limitation (short-to-long sequence generalization in recurrent models). However, it is a restatement of others' work with low engagement (14 likes), and Burkov is a curator here rather than the researcher.
items.summary_html: Burkov summarizes an Adobe research article on long-context training for recurrent architectures, explaining how learning signals propagate over time and introducing a technique called Credit Stabilization through Time to stabilize state credit so models trained on short sequences generalize to longer contexts.

Text-to-Speech models ...
items.content:
This is the first audio model I've seen that lets you edit individual words.

Text-to-Speech models have gotten really good lately, but they still make mistakes, and I hate having to redo an entire voiceover because one word is wrong.

@FishAudio just released Drama 3, and it supports audio inpainting.

Basically, you can regenerate a word or phrase inside your audio while keeping everything else unchanged.

The workflow is simple:

1. Generate your voiceover
2. Choose the word or phrase you want to replace
3. Generate the replacement and keep the rest of the take

It works surprisingly well!

By the way, you can do this in 83+ languages!

Thanks to the Fish Audio team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
Grok Bot can now claim its own email address, so we tested it with several project emails, one of which changed a deadline.

It caught the new date, summarized what changed, and drafted a reply marked "Needs approval."

items.summary_html: The Forecasting Research Institute responds to methodological scrutiny of an aggregate finding of a 20% increase in expert forecasts, explaining that the headline result depends on a minority view, that alternative individual-level aggregation for EA-affiliated experts yields a median difference near zero, and that the sample of 38 has wide bootstrap confidence intervals.
items.content_html:
@ben_j_todd @GabrielDunin @EzraKarger 2. Our aggregate result of “20% increase” is made possible by the existence of this minority view, but two methodological factors also contribute:

2b. To produce our top-line aggregate results, we compared each group’s aggregate median under a policy condition with its aggregate median in the unconditional case. We could also have compared at the individual level and taken the median of these differences. Doing so yields a median difference among EA-affiliated experts just below 0.

2c. 38 is a relatively small sample. We update the figure below with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, which are quite wide for the EA-affiliated estimates. Sampling noise could easily have made this point estimate negative (or more positive).

items.content_html:
@ben_j_todd @GabrielDunin @EzraKarger 1. Among the 38 EA-affiliated experts who completed this survey, 10 forecast higher risk under US-only pre-release restrictions than under the unconditional case

Their rationales often cite the fact that they expect some effective safety policies to be implemented in the unconditional world, reducing the baseline risk against which each policy is compared.

Several then argue that internally deployed models pose more risk than released models. Release restrictions could then mean each model spends more time behind closed doors and unavailable to external safety/security research, potentially increasing risk.

items.content_html:
@ben_j_todd @GabrielDunin @EzraKarger See the figures below for details. Overall, we still think the conclusion that EA-affiliated experts hold similar views is justified. There may be differences, but they are not large enough to be statistically distinguishable, especially with our relatively small sample. And the share of each group supporting each policy is remarkably similar.

Specific point estimates, though, should be taken with a grain of salt, and we can do better to emphasize that in the future.

For now, we still find this minority viewpoint interesting and potentially worth exploring further! Curious to hear if you agree!

Claude Beyond the Prompt — Build reusable skills and agentic workflows: https://t.co/eFtur83h1L

To be released soon by @PacktPublishing — You can order now with the very favorable Amazon price guarantee.

Amazon Description:
“Claude is powerful, but many people use it in fragile, one-off ways. You prompt, get an answer, and move on. Real work, however, is not a single prompt; it is a sequence of tasks, decisions, and context.

This book shows you how to move from prompts to skills and toward true agentic engineering. Instead of refining prompts, you will learn a practical, structured way of working with AI by designing skills and workflows that produce consistent results and can be tested, improved, and reused.

Rather than teaching you to rely on tools that quickly become outdated, this book helps build a durable mental model for working with AI. By the end, you will not just prompt AI but design how work is carried out with it, using Claude or any AI tool of your choice.”

The add-on bouncer

Patrick built agent-guard, a free tool that checks the add-ons you give AI agents like Claude Code and Codex for malware and password theft before they install.

It runs security scanners from NVIDIA, Cisco, and Datadog, returns a plain safe-or-blocked verdict, and installs only the exact version it checked.

items.title: One more high-quality non-English textbook that I converted and translated from French into English ...
items.content:
One more high-quality non-English textbook that I converted and translated from French into English for the ever growing @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks:

Combinational and Sequential Logic Circuits by Guy Bégin (2023) is an introductory textbook for technical-education and undergraduate students, as well as readers interested in electronic engineering.

It assumes no prior knowledge of the subject; programming experience is useful, but not required, for the later simulation work.

The book presents logic-circuit design as a foundation of digital electronic systems, concentrating on how binary information is represented, processed, stored, and tested.

Its focus is digital logic rather than analog electronics or the transistor-level construction of devices.

The textbook has 107 pages, 211 illustrations, and 62 exercises that were adapted to work with an AI tutor that guides you instead of giving you the full solution.

items.content_html:
One more high-quality non-English textbook that I converted and translated from French into English for the ever growing @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks:

Combinational and Sequential Logic Circuits by Guy Bégin (2023) is an introductory textbook for technical-education and undergraduate students, as well as readers interested in electronic engineering.

It assumes no prior knowledge of the subject; programming experience is useful, but not required, for the later simulation work.

The book presents logic-circuit design as a foundation of digital electronic systems, concentrating on how binary information is represented, processed, stored, and tested.

Its focus is digital logic rather than analog electronics or the transistor-level construction of devices.

The textbook has 107 pages, 211 illustrations, and 62 exercises that were adapted to work with an AI tutor that guides you instead of giving you the full solution.

Enjoy: https://t.co/AYmqKZrVBx

items.content:
Is the connected travel ecosystem rewriting business travel?

AI is beginning to change more than how people book a flight or submit an expense report. When travel data, supplier content, workflows, and intelligence are connected, the potential is a more personalized, proactive, policy-compliant traveler experience, with less manual work for employees and managers.

In my latest CXO Spice conversation, Paul Dear, SVP of Cocnur Travel at @SAPConcur, and I discuss what it will take to get clean data, meaningful use cases, people-centered adoption, and governance that creates trust.

Read #CXOSpice newsletter: https://t.co/Pou13wK2Gl
